opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's a pleasure to be here.

I think it's a major leap because, for decades, robotics has been stuck in a world of narrow, hand-engineered intelligence. A traditional industrial robot is very precise and very reliable, but only within an extremely constrained environment. You program it for one task, welding a car door or picking a particular part from a bin, and if anything changes, the lighting, the position of the object, the shape of the object, it fails. Every new task meant new code, new data, new tuning. That doesn't scale.

What foundation models bring is generalization. Look at what happened with language. Before large models, we had separate systems for translation, for question answering, for summarization, each trained on its own dataset. Then one large pre-trained model could do all of these, and many things we never explicitly trained it for. The same shift is now starting in the physical world. A robot foundation model, trained on huge amounts of vision, language, and action data, can begin to understand a scene, follow a natural-language instruction, reason about what it needs to do, and turn that into motor actions, even in situations it hasn't seen before.

So I usually describe it as moving from information intelligence to physical intelligence. The first wave of AI lived mostly on the internet: text, images, search, recommendations. The next wave is AI that has a body, that can perceive, move, and act in the real world. That's what we call embodied intelligence, and the foundation model is like giving the robot a brain with common sense instead of a set of scripts.

That said, I want to be realistic. The physical world is much harder than the digital world. Data is scarcer and more expensive to collect, because you can't just scrape the internet for robot actions. Safety requirements are much higher, since a mistake in a chatbot is an embarrassing sentence, but a mistake in a robot or a car can hurt someone. And the loop between perception, decision, and action must run in real time. So we'll need a lot of simulation, synthetic data, and real-world deployment working together, much like what we did in autonomous driving.

But the direction is clear. Once robots have a general-purpose brain, the cost of teaching them a new skill drops dramatically, and that's when you get the kind of explosion we saw with smartphones or the internet. I believe that over the next ten years, robots, including humanoids, household robots, and industrial robots, could become one of the biggest applications of AI, and the foundation model is the key that unlocks it.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot can follow a natural-language instruction, but does not specify that the instruction is spoken.

r002.rationale: It says the robot can reason about what it needs to do and turn a natural-language instruction into motor actions.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a leap because, for the first time, the robot's "brain" can be separated from its "body." Historically, robotics was a hardware problem first and a software problem second. Every robot was programmed for a specific task, in a specific environment, with a specific body. You'd spend months tuning a robotic arm to pick up a particular kind of part, and if the lighting changed or the part changed, it broke. The intelligence was brittle and it didn't transfer.

What large models change is that you now have a general representation of the world, of language, of physical common sense, that was learned from enormous amounts of data, and you can put that into the robot. So the robot doesn't start from zero. It already understands that a cup is something you hold by the handle, that a door opens one way, that if I say "clean up the table" it means a sequence of actions, not one action. The foundation model gives it perception, reasoning, and task decomposition in one package, and then the embodiment-specific part, the control, the low-level motor skills, becomes a much thinner layer.

I often compare it to what happened with autonomous driving. In the early days we had separate modules for perception, prediction, planning, each hand-engineered. Then end-to-end learning came and collapsed those into one model, and the capability jumped. Robotics is going through the same transition, except the problem is broader, because a car has basically one task and one body, while a general robot has to handle an open-ended set of tasks across many bodies.

The other reason I call it a leap is the data flywheel. Once the brain is general, every robot deployed in the world becomes a data collector for every other robot. That's how you get from thousands of units to millions. Without a shared model, each deployment is an island. With it, the whole fleet learns together.

Now, I want to be careful. We are still early. Physical data is scarce compared to text, the real world is unforgiving of mistakes, and the gap between a demo and a reliable product is large. But the direction is clear. The brain is being built, and I think over the next five to ten years, embodied intelligence will be the largest application of AI after language models themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot understands what “clean up the table” means when instructed, linking language understanding to the user’s spoken instruction.

r002.rationale: It says the model provides task decomposition and interprets “clean up the table” as a sequence of actions for the robot.

astra-6.text:
I think the major leap is that we move from programming a robot for one specific task to giving it a general foundation for understanding and acting. Traditionally, if you change the task or the environment, you often have to do a great deal of engineering again. A foundation model offers the possibility of transferring what the robot has learned across tasks.

For example, you could tell a robot, “Please clear the table,” rather than specify every movement. It needs to recognize the objects, understand what clearing the table means, plan the actions, and adjust if something unexpected happens. That brings perception, language, reasoning, and action together.

Of course, understanding an instruction is not the same as executing it reliably. The physical world requires precision, and mistakes can have real consequences. But this gives us a path toward robots that can learn new skills and adapt to new situations, instead of repeating only what we explicitly programmed.

r001.rationale: The response says the robot can understand what “clear the table” means, but it does not specify that the instruction is spoken.

r002.rationale: It says the robot can receive a high-level request and plan the actions needed, rather than having every movement specified.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the major leap is that we move from programming a robot for one specific task to giving it a general foundation for learning many tasks. Traditionally, you might build a robot that performs very well in a factory, but when you change the environment or the task, you have to do a lot of engineering again.

A foundation model offers the possibility of connecting perception, language, reasoning, and action. You can tell the robot what you want to accomplish, and it can use what it has learned to interpret the situation and work out how to act.

Of course, understanding an instruction is different from executing it safely in the physical world. That remains a very difficult challenge. But the potential is significant: instead of developing each capability separately, we can build on a shared model that helps robots adapt to new tasks and environments.

r001.rationale: The response says users can tell the robot what they want and it can interpret the situation, but it does not specify spoken instructions.

r002.rationale: The response says the robot can work out how to act, but does not state that it breaks a high-level instruction into executable actions.
